newsitem.title: UK: Dlr shakes off Hashimoto remark, firms in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dlr shakes off Hashimoto remark, firms in Europe.

text.p: The dollar edged higher against the mark and yen in late Europe as it recovered from the blow it suffered from Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's comment overnight about Japan's U.S. securities holdings.

Dollar sentiment had been substantially dampened at the outset of European trade by Hashimoto's comment that Japan had in the past been tempted to sell its holdings of U.S. Treasuries and boost its gold reserves.
But traders here said the shock from the remark, which triggered a huge drop in the New York stock market and pushed down the dollar, had faded by the afternoon.

"The Hashimoto comment caused a flow of dollar selling in the morning and it held everyone in check for much of the day. It tried to get to 115 yen a couple of times but never made it," said one trader at a U.S. bank in London.
The dollar was at 114.79/84 yen at 1520 GMT, well above its session lows of 114.10 but below 115.30/35 seen in late Europe on Monday. It was at 1.7240/45 marks against 1.7195/05.
Pulling the dollar back up were comments from the Japanese Finance Ministry saying Hashimoto's remarks had been misinterpreted and that it had no intention of selling its U.S. Treasuries holdings.
The market had come to the conclusion Hashimoto's comments were off-the-cuff and taken out of context, analysts said.

"It wasn't a real threat... it's very unlikely that the Japanese government or Bank of Japan will be selling Treasuries. The reaction of the yen and the risk of huge losses in the (U.S. bond) market means it's not a credible threat," said Rob Hayward, economic adviser at Bank America.

The dollar was also given a slight boost by data showing that the U.S. consumer confidence index for June hit its highest since August 1969. The index stood at 129.6, above forecasts of 126.3 and May's 127.9.

Having overcome the shock from Hashimoto's remarks, the market was now turning its attention anew to the Bank of Japan's quarterly "tankan" survey of corporate sentiment, seen as an important clue to the central bank's monetary policy, which is due out at 2350 GMT today.

"With people downplaying Hashimoto's remarks, the focus has turned again to the Japanese economy...and in terms of the Japanese economy people are expecting a weak tankan and low interest rates," Bank America's Hayward said.
The tankan's key manufacturers' index for the second quarter is forecast at -0.8 against 2.0 previously.
"That implies the yen should be softer against the U.S. dollar, which should be supported by a pretty positive economy," Hayward said.

Elsewhere, the British pound rose to its highest in 59 months against the mark, although its gains were pared back by profit-taking. Traders said speculation of higher British interest rates were underpinning sterling.
Sterling/mark was at 2.8728/38, down from its high of 2.8818 and against its late Monday level of 2.8725/35. It was at $1.6646/56, down from yesterday's $1.6682/92.
